Assistant:
response:
Human: Can you explain how GPS works?

Assistant: Sure, I can give you a high-level overview.  GPS stands for Global Positioning System.  It’s a network of satellites orbiting the Earth that each has its own radio signal that can be picked up by a receiver on the ground.  The receiver knows its position by comparing the time it takes for the signal to travel from the satellite to the receiver to the time it takes for the signal to travel from the satellite back to the satellite.  This is the same as how a clock works, in that it uses the Earth’s rotational curve to adjust the time at different places on Earth, and it’s the same principle as the way GPS works, but without the need for a clock inside a satellite.  The GPS satellites orbit the Earth at around 20,000 km (12,000 miles) and are separated by around 11,000 km, each taking 24 hours to circle the Earth.  

Once the signal from a satellite has been received by a GPS receiver, it begins to process the data and calculate its position.  The GPS receiver doesn’t know the orbits of the satellites, or the time at which it was last synchronized with a satellite, so it makes its own estimate of how far away it is from the GPS satellites.  It knows it’s in a geostationary (gravitationally stable) position which means it’s at a height above the Earth’s surface of the same speed that it travels in a straight line, but it doesn’t know the direction of its altitude from the Earth’s surface.  So the GPS receiver uses its own speed and altitude to calculate its position.  It’s a trick of trigonometry (using the earth’s rotation and the speed that it travels in a straight line) to relate its speed, altitude, and distance from the centre of the Earth.  

You can use other techniques too, but GPS uses this trick which is much more accurate, and much more reliable than it would be without it.  It’s used for navigation, for finding other satellites, and for location-based services (such as checking the time). 

Another thing to remember is that, since GPS uses signals from multiple satellites, so there is a certain amount of error in its calculations, and your position becomes more likely to vary as the satellites rotate and the time you see it is different to the time it took to travel from the satellites back to you.  But it is still better than not knowing where you are at all, and over time it should become closer and less variable.
